parts.title: Getting up at five
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Last autumn, I decided to change my routine and get up at five every morning. Everyone told me that the early hours are the best time to work, and I wanted to see if it was true.

The first week was a disaster. I set my alarm for 5 a.m., but every morning I turned it off and went back to sleep. In the end, my sister suggested a trick: she told me to put the alarm on the other side of the room. When I had to get out of bed to stop the noise, I was awake.

After two weeks, it became easier. At that time of day, the world is silent, and I could write, go for a run or just have breakfast in peace. My neighbours were still asleep, my phone was quiet, and nobody needed anything from me.

However, there was a price. I was so tired in the evenings that I could not stay awake after nine o'clock, so I stopped seeing my friends on weekdays. After two months, I changed my plan to six o'clock. It is not as magical as five, but I still have the quiet time, and I have my evenings back.

questions.prompt: Why did the writer try getting up at five?
options: To finish a book before winter
To test what people told her
Because her sister asked her to
Because her job began very early
questions.explanation: People told her that early hours are the best time to work, and she wanted to see if it was true.

questions.prompt: What went wrong in the first week?
options: She turned off her alarm each day
She could not find her alarm clock
She was ill for several days
Her neighbours woke her too early
questions.explanation: She turned off the alarm every morning and went back to sleep.

questions.prompt: How did she solve the problem?
options: By going to bed much earlier
By using an alarm on her phone
By asking her sister to wake her
questions.explanation: Her sister told her to put the alarm on the other side of the room.

questions.prompt: What did she like about the early hours?
options: She could talk to her friends
questions.explanation: The world was silent, and nobody needed anything from her.

questions.prompt: Why did she change to six o'clock?
options: Her sister got up later than she did
She was too tired at night
The mornings were too dark to run
Her neighbours complained of the noise
questions.explanation: She was too tired to stay awake after nine, so she stopped seeing her friends.

parts.title: The night bus driver
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
At eleven o'clock at night, when most people are going to bed, Mina Torres is starting work. She drives the number 24 night bus through the city, and she has been doing it for eight years. [1] Her family says that she lives 'upside down', but she says she loves it.

Mina sleeps from nine in the morning until four in the afternoon. [2] She puts thick curtains on her bedroom window and turns off her phone, so that nothing can wake her. After she gets up, she cooks dinner for her children, who are just coming home from school.

Her passengers are very different from those in the day. [3] Some are nurses going home after a long shift, and others are students who have missed the last train. 'A few of them fall asleep and miss their stop,' she laughs. [4] She always checks the seats at the end of the line before she leaves.

The worst part is winter, when the weather is cold and the streets are empty. [5] But Mina says that she would not change her job. 'At night, the city belongs to us,' she says.
sentences: Her children are fast asleep when she leaves for work.
Others forget things, such as umbrellas, bags and sometimes even shoes.
Getting enough sleep in the daytime is difficult, so she has learned a few tricks.
It is not an easy timetable, because she finishes at seven in the morning.
Sometimes the heating on the bus breaks, and everyone feels cold until the end of the line.
Few buses run after midnight in small towns.
There are far fewer of them, and they are usually tired and quiet.
She learned to drive when she was twenty, in her father's old truck.

gaps.explanation: The sentence explains that her timetable is hard, and the next sentence says that her family thinks she lives upside down.
The sentence says that daytime sleep is difficult, and the next sentence describes her tricks with curtains and her phone.
The sentence says that night passengers are fewer and quieter, and the next sentence gives examples of who they are.
The sentence says that other passengers forget things, which is why she checks the seats at the end of the line.
The sentence gives another winter problem, and the next sentence says that Mina would still not change her job.

parts.title: Sleeping better
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage:
Many teenagers do not get enough sleep, which can make it hard to [1] attention at school. Experts say that young people need about nine hours a night. One of the easiest ways to improve your sleep is to go to bed [2] the same time every evening. Try to avoid screens for an hour before bed, because the light from them tells your brain that it is still daytime. A warm shower or a quiet book can help you [3] down.

It is also a good idea to keep your room cool and dark. Finally, do not drink coffee or cola in the evening, because they [4] caffeine, which keeps you awake. If you still cannot sleep after twenty minutes, get up and do something [5], like listening to soft music, until you feel [6].

questions.prompt: Gap 1
questions.explanation: The fixed expression is "pay attention".

questions.prompt: Gap 2
questions.explanation: We say "at the same time".

questions.prompt: Gap 3
questions.explanation: To "wind down" means to relax after a busy day.

questions.prompt: Gap 4
questions.explanation: Coffee and cola contain caffeine.

questions.prompt: Gap 5
questions.explanation: The adjective "relaxing" describes the activity, such as soft music.

questions.prompt: Gap 6
questions.explanation: You feel sleepy before you fall asleep.

parts.title: A message about my day
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage:
Hi Jonas,
Thanks for your email. You asked [1] my daily routine, so here it is! On school days, I get up at half past six and [2] a quick shower. Then I have breakfast with my brother, and we catch the bus at ten to eight. I usually get home [3] four o'clock. After that, I do my homework, and [4] the weather is good, I go for a run before dinner. We eat at seven, and I am usually in bed [5] ten. At the weekends, I sleep much later! What time do you [6] up on Saturdays?
Write soon,
Hanne

gaps.explanation: We say "have a shower" or "take a shower".
She usually gets home at or by four o'clock.
The run depends on the weather, so "if" or "when" fits.
"In bed by ten" means no later than ten, and "at ten" is also possible.
"Get up" or "wake up" asks about the time you leave your bed.

parts.title: Short conversations
parts.instructions: Listen to seven short conversations. Choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: estelle
turns.text: Dane, I have to set my alarm. My train to Leeds leaves at eight.

turns.speaker: dane
turns.text: So you’ll get up at five, like last time?

turns.speaker: estelle
turns.text: Last time I was so tired that I nearly fell asleep on the platform. The station is only twenty minutes away, and I can have toast on the train, so I don’t need all that time.

turns.speaker: dane
turns.text: Then shall I put in seven? That gives you an hour.

turns.speaker: estelle
turns.text: Seven o’clock is too late. I still have to pack my laptop and find my ticket. I want an hour before that.

turns.speaker: dane
turns.text: OK, I’ll set it on your phone. Don’t blame me if you hate it!

question.prompt: What time will Estelle set her alarm?
question.explanation: Five was the time of last time and seven was rejected as too late; she wants one hour before seven.

turns.speaker: isaura
turns.text: Wallace, you look tired. Do you still watch films in bed?

turns.speaker: wallace
turns.text: I used to, on my phone, but the screen kept me awake, so I stopped. Then I tried a book. I read three pages and fell asleep with the light on, which is not very comfortable, so that idea is out too.

turns.speaker: isaura
turns.text: So what do you do now?

turns.speaker: wallace
turns.text: My grandfather had a little radio next to his bed, so I bought one. I put on a quiet talking programme, and the voices make me sleepy. Ten minutes and I’m gone.

He watches a film on his phone

turns.speaker: brigitta
turns.text: Hello, this is Brigitta from flat twelve, leaving a message for the building manager. I’m calling about the problems on our floor. The lift was out of order last week, but it has been repaired and works well now. The stairs are not very clean either, although the cleaner told me she comes on Mondays, so I’ll wait for that. But what really bothers me is what happens after midnight. Somebody in the flat below plays music so loudly that my bed shakes, and I have to get up at six for work. I’ve asked them twice, nicely, to turn it down. Please speak to them this week. Call me back on my mobile. Thanks very much.

options: A broken lift in the building

turns.speaker: cassia
turns.text: Benedict, do you always have breakfast at your desk? I saw you with a sandwich yesterday.

turns.speaker: benedict
turns.text: That was a one-off. Yesterday I had a meeting at eight, so I ate at the office. Normally I’d love to eat at home, but my kids take forever, and I have to leave at seven to catch my train.

turns.speaker: cassia
turns.text: So you don’t have time at all?

turns.speaker: benedict
turns.text: I do, actually. I buy a coffee and a croissant at the station and eat them in my seat, looking out of the window. It’s the quietest part of my day.

question.explanation: Yesterday was a one-off at the office and he cannot stay at home, but he eats his croissant in his seat after he catches the train.

turns.speaker: madge
turns.text: You look terrible, Rhett. Did you sleep well?

turns.speaker: rhett
turns.text: Not really. I went to bed at eleven, which is early for me, and I thought I’d get six hours at least.

turns.speaker: madge
turns.text: So what happened?

turns.speaker: rhett
turns.text: The neighbours’ baby cried from midnight. I finally fell asleep around two, and my alarm went off at six. At the weekend I usually sleep for ten hours, so this is a big shock.

turns.speaker: madge
turns.text: Poor you. Have a strong tea.

question.prompt: How long did Rhett sleep last night?
question.explanation: He hoped for six hours and sleeps ten at the weekend, but he fell asleep at two and woke up at six.

turns.speaker: dermot
turns.text: Nessa, why do you go to work at five? Surely that’s too early.

turns.speaker: nessa
turns.text: I thought so too at first. The bus tickets are cheaper before six, but that isn’t why I do it. I’d happily pay more. And you can smell the fresh bread from the bakery near the market, though I never buy anything at that time because the shop isn’t open.

turns.speaker: dermot
turns.text: So what’s the attraction?

turns.speaker: nessa
turns.text: Nobody is around. No cars, no crowds, just me and a few birds. The streets are so quiet that it feels as if the whole city belongs to me, and I can think in peace.

turns.speaker: dermot
turns.text: I prefer my bed, honestly.

question.prompt: What does Nessa like about early mornings?
question.explanation: The cheaper tickets are not her reason and the bakery is closed; she enjoys the calm, empty streets.

turns.speaker: pauline

turns.speaker: kenny
turns.text: I’ll book the tickets online, but I’ll do that on the bus later.

turns.speaker: pauline
turns.text: Shall we eat first?

turns.speaker: kenny
turns.text: There isn’t time for a proper dinner. We’ll grab a pizza after the film. Before anything else, I’ve promised to take my little sister to the pool. She has a swimming lesson at six, and I’m her lift.

turns.speaker: pauline
turns.text: Oh, OK. Then I’ll meet you at the cinema.

turns.speaker: kenny
turns.text: Perfect. I’ll see you at quarter to nine.

turns.speaker: yvaine

turns.speaker: bertil
turns.text: Do you lie there looking at the clock?

parts.title: A sleep workshop
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: leona
turns.text: Good evening, and welcome to our sleep workshop at the Riverside Health Centre. My name is Leona, and I’m a nurse here. Today I’ll give you five simple ideas, and we’ll finish at about eight o’clock. First, regular habits. Many people think the important thing is to sleep for eight hours, but the body also likes a pattern. So choose one time to go to bed, and stay with it every night. I know many of you relax on Sundays, but keep the pattern even on Saturdays, because that is the night that breaks it. Second, the room. Some of my patients buy an expensive mattress, and of course that can help, but it is better to start with the light. The television is easy to turn off. But even a small light from a phone charger can wake the brain, so make the room as dark as you can. Heavy curtains are fine, or a sleeping mask. Third, food. A big dinner late in the evening is a bad idea. Some people say a hot chocolate is the best thing before bed, but I prefer something light, for example a banana. Cheese can give strange dreams, so I wouldn’t eat it. Fourth, exercise. It is excellent for sleep, but timing matters. Some websites say you should stop one hour before bed, but I’d leave two, because your body is still warm and awake. A walk in the afternoon, or even in the morning, is much better. Fifth, worries. Lots of people lie in bed thinking about tomorrow. Keep a notebook by the bed, and put your worries on a piece of paper. I don’t mean on your phone, because the screen is bright. Then you can leave them until the morning. Finally, an announcement. Next Tuesday at seven we have another workshop, about how children sleep. Parents, please bring your questions. The one after that, in two weeks, will be about older people. Thank you, and sleep well.

gaps.explanation: She says to keep the pattern on Saturdays, the night that breaks it, even though many people relax on Sundays.

gaps.prompt: A small light from a ___ can wake the brain
gaps.explanation: The television is easy to turn off, but a small light from a phone charger can wake the brain.

gaps.prompt: A good snack before bed is a ___
gaps.explanation: She prefers something light, a banana, instead of hot chocolate, and she would not eat cheese.
Some websites say one hour, but she would leave two hours.

gaps.prompt: Put your worries on a piece of ___
gaps.explanation: She says to keep a notebook but to put worries on a piece of paper, not on the phone.

gaps.prompt: Next Tuesday: a workshop on how ___ sleep
gaps.explanation: The workshop next Tuesday is about how children sleep; the one in two weeks is about older people.

parts.title: A sleep scientist
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: ivor
turns.text: Elowen, welcome. Why did you become a sleep scientist?

turns.speaker: elowen
turns.text: People expect a family story. My parents were teachers, so it wasn’t that, and I did read a famous book about dreams, but I had already chosen my subject by then. The real reason is that I couldn’t sleep for weeks before my exams at university. I was so frustrated that I wanted to understand what was happening in my own head.

turns.speaker: ivor
turns.text: Let’s talk about teenagers. Are they lazy?

turns.speaker: elowen
turns.text: That annoys me. Their body clock moves about two hours later during these years, so they truly aren’t sleepy at ten. Some parents say the answer is an earlier bedtime, and some schools talk about starting the day later. Both ideas have something in their favour, and I understand why teachers argue about it, but what I mind is the word lazy. It is biology, not character.

turns.speaker: ivor
turns.text: What about sleeping late at the weekend?

turns.speaker: elowen
turns.text: Many of us do it, and it does feel wonderful. It repays a little of the missing sleep, but it moves your body clock, so on Sunday night you can’t fall asleep and Monday is hard. It doesn’t cure everything, and it isn’t dangerous for the brain either. It’s a small help with a price, so I try to wake up within an hour of my normal time, even on a holiday. My friends think I’m boring, but I feel much better on Mondays.

turns.speaker: ivor
turns.text: And afternoon naps?

turns.speaker: elowen
turns.text: I’m a fan, as long as they’re short. Twenty minutes is perfect. After an hour you wake up heavy and confused, and then you won’t sleep at night. I would never tell anybody to forbid naps, though. Plenty of people can’t take one at all, and that’s fine.

turns.speaker: ivor
turns.text: You travel a lot. How do you deal with jet lag?

turns.speaker: elowen
turns.text: I tried the strong coffee trick for years, and it only left me nervous. Sleeping for a long time in the afternoon makes it worse, because then the night is wide awake. What works for me is going outside and walking in the daylight, even if I’m tired. The light tells your body what time it is.

turns.speaker: ivor
turns.text: Finally, what is your best advice? Imagine you can only give one tip.

turns.speaker: elowen
turns.text: Put your phone away before bed, and I mean off, not just silent. Everyone says go to bed at nine, but a fixed time is not the same for everybody. Some say sleep with the window open, which is nice and fresh, but it’s not the secret. The phone is the biggest enemy.
